classification.tone: heightened, melodramatic, cruelly comic, and aggressively violent

evaluation.positioning_hook: A bullied teen friend group is hunted by a killer tied to their past prank, while one girl’s missing grandmother turns the whole school into a suspect pool.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has a clean horror engine, teen relationship drama, and a built-in mystery around the killer’s identity, which gives it a clear genre audience. The friend-group dynamics and school setting make the emotional promise easy to grasp, even as the script leans into a very specific, high-intensity teen voice.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The central setup is legible: a group of teens connected to a cruel prank becomes the target of a masked killer, with Sammy’s grandmother and the earlier Katie murder forming the spine of the mystery. The script keeps introducing new turns and relationships, so the hook is there, but it arrives through a lot of moving parts.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Sammy, Faye, Austin, Lauren, and Lucy each have a strong behavioral signature, and the script gives them distinct social rhythms that actors can play. The characters are built more as loud, specific types than as deeply layered contradictions, but the ensemble has enough personality to carry a feature.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script commits hard to a maximalist teen-horror soap opera mode, with blunt dialogue, extreme violence, and a very specific social ecosystem. The boldness is in the volume and the willingness to make every scene emotionally and verbally overcooked, which gives it a recognizable edge even when the underlying setup is familiar.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script is constantly in motion, with murders, interrogations, relationship blowups, and repeated chase sequences keeping the pages active. The momentum comes from escalation and shock rather than clean suspense architecture, so it stays busy and readable, but the feature shape is more episodic than tightly engineered.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The killer-on-the-loose framework is familiar, but the script’s specific teen-group banter, the grandmother angle, and the social-media-era friend drama give it a distinct surface. What makes it memorable is the intensity of the voice and the sheer specificity of the interpersonal chaos rather than a wholly new premise.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The world is rooted in a high school, family homes, a police station, and a party circuit, with enough social texture to suggest a lived-in teen ecosystem. The school hierarchy, family dynamics, and public aftermath of the murders create a usable world, though the setting functions more as a pressure cooker than a fully layered system.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is unmistakably heightened: grief, jealousy, flirtation, and slasher violence all play at full volume, often in the same scene. The script has a very particular voice—abrasive, funny, romantic, and cruel—which makes it easy to identify from a page or two.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are seeds of deeper material in Lucy’s isolation, Sammy’s attachment patterns, and the group’s cruelty toward outsiders, but the script mostly stays on the surface of immediate conflict and reaction. The emotional material is present, yet the feature plays more as a chain of events than as a slow reveal of hidden interiority.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The script is powered by a web of pairings—Sammy/Lucy, Austin/Lauren, Faye/Daniel, Julia/Austin, and the shifting group allegiance around Eric and Ryan. Those relationships generate constant friction, jealousy, and loyalty tests, which gives the ensemble real story fuel.

casting_characteristics: Multiple female and male roles in the 17-18 range
One family unit with parents and siblings

technical.vfx_details: Primarily practical violence and cleanup shots; any gore or body-disposal beats would be handled with modest effects work.
technical.sfx_needs: Knife attacks, gunshots, falls, chokeholds, and repeated chase choreography drive the action.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model; the engine is a teen slasher mystery built around a killer targeting a friend group after a past prank.

cost.note: Contemporary school-and-home settings, a small cast footprint, and mostly practical violence keep the budget naturally contained.

cast.note: The script depends on a sizable teen ensemble with specific age ranges and strong chemistry across multiple pairings.

location.note: The story stays in a manageable set of contemporary locations: school, homes, police station, restaurant, and park.

content.note: Graphic stabbing, throat-slitting, gunshots, profanity, bullying, and sexualized teen dialogue push the material into mature territory.

rights.note: The script uses a few named brands and a film reference, but no major IP dependency or life-rights requirement is apparent.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The killer is tied to a social wound.
strengths.what_it_means: This is not random-body-count horror; the violence grows out of a specific teen social ecosystem, which gives the murders emotional charge and makes the mystery feel personal. That kind of motive-driven slasher premise is easier to market because the audience understands the emotional engine immediately.
strengths.evidence: Katie’s death is linked to the group’s prank history, and the grandmother’s warning frames the danger as coming from inside the friend circle’s past.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ensemble has loud, playable identities.
strengths.what_it_means: Each teen has a distinct social rhythm—Sammy’s party-girl defiance, Faye’s nonstop verbal overflow, Austin’s polished confidence, Lauren’s romantic intensity, Lucy’s isolation, Eric’s quietness. That gives casting a real hook and gives the movie a built-in group dynamic that can generate scenes, not just plot.
strengths.evidence: The cafeteria scenes and the repeated group conversations give every character a recognizable verbal signature.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The script commits to a feral teen voice.
strengths.what_it_means: The dialogue is unapologetically heightened, messy, funny, and confrontational, which gives the piece a strong identity in the crowded teen-horror space. It feels designed to be performed with attitude, speed, and volatility.
strengths.evidence: The cafeteria banter, the interrogations, and the breakup arguments all run on the same combustible energy.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The grandmother angle gives the mystery a signature face.
strengths.what_it_means: A killer linked to an escaped grandmother in a mental facility is a memorable hook that immediately separates the story from faceless masked-slasher material. It also gives the film a built-in mythology that can be teased, revealed, and escalated.
strengths.evidence: Sammy’s earlier attack, the police mention of the escaped grandmother, and the later reveal at the party all point to the same threat.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The relationships are the engine, not just decoration.
strengths.what_it_means: The script keeps turning romance, friendship, jealousy, and betrayal into survival pressure, which makes the horror feel socially alive. That’s valuable commercially because it broadens the appeal beyond gore fans into viewers who want relationship drama with stakes.
strengths.evidence: Austin/Lauren/Julia, Sammy/Lucy, and Faye/Daniel all drive major turns in the story.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The violence is staged as escalation, not background.
strengths.what_it_means: The attacks are frequent, direct, and increasingly personal, which keeps the movie in motion and gives the feature a clear forward drive. For the right producer, that means a clean genre promise with strong trailer moments.
strengths.evidence: Katie’s home invasion, Julia’s house massacre, Faye’s chase, and the party attack all escalate the danger in distinct set pieces.

whats_special.headline: This is a loud, mean, highly playable teen slasher with a real social engine: a friend group’s past cruelty comes back as a body-count mystery. The script’s biggest asset is its ensemble voice — every character is sharply coded, emotionally combustible, and built for actors who want something big to do.

lead_characters.name: Sammy Miller
lead_characters.hook: Sammy is the social center of the movie: party-forward, defensive, funny, and always one beat away from either cracking a joke or starting a fight. She carries herself like someone who wants to be untouchable, but the script keeps exposing how much she needs loyalty, control, and proof that her people are still hers. She’s the kind of lead who can be abrasive and sympathetic in the same breath, which makes her a strong horror anchor.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a showcase role for a young actor who can play speed, attitude, and emotional whiplash without losing audience sympathy. The part has the volatility of a lead in a teen thriller and the social command of a sharp ensemble player, with room for both confrontation and vulnerability in the same scene. It lives in the same performance neighborhood as the raw, defensive energy of a strong teen-drama lead in a horror frame.

lead_characters.name: Faye Woodbridge
lead_characters.hook: Faye is a human firehose: talkative, theatrical, needy, funny, and deeply sensitive under the noise. The script uses her as both comic pressure valve and emotional detonator, which makes her one of the most distinctive roles in the piece. She’s the kind of character who can dominate a room and then collapse in private, and that contrast gives the part real actor appeal.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a juicy role for an actor who can weaponize energy and then turn on a dime into grief. The part offers big comedic rhythm, romantic play, and full-throttle panic, with a late-story emotional lane that can land hard. It has the kind of expressive volatility that recalls the showy, scene-stealing side of a horror ensemble performance.

lead_characters.name: Austin Moore
lead_characters.hook: Austin is the polished, confident, socially fluent guy who thinks he can manage every room he enters. He’s romantic, strategic, and a little self-satisfied, but the script also lets him reveal real loyalty and leadership when the crisis hits. He functions as the group’s stabilizer, which makes him a useful counterweight to the more chaotic personalities around him.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a strong role for a charismatic young actor who can play charm as a tool and sincerity as a surprise. The part gives him romance, authority, and a few sharp confrontational beats, which makes it attractive for someone looking to lead a genre ensemble without disappearing into the background. It has the clean, confident energy of a teen lead who can carry both the social and suspense sides of the movie.

lead_characters.name: Lauren Cheng
lead_characters.hook: Lauren is observant, emotionally intelligent, and quietly strategic, the kind of character who listens more than she speaks and then lands the truth when it matters. She’s also deeply romantic, which gives her a soft center inside a very controlled exterior. That combination makes her feel like the smartest person in the room without turning her into a cold cipher.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a great part for an actor who can play intelligence, restraint, and romantic longing with precision. Lauren gets to be the emotional translator in the ensemble, the girlfriend, the confidante, and the one who sees through the noise, which is a strong showcase in a crowded teen cast. The role has the grounded, watchful quality that often stands out in ensemble thrillers.

lead_characters.name: Lucy
lead_characters.hook: Lucy is the quiet outsider with a sharp edge, and the script gives her a lot of emotional pressure without making her generic. She’s isolated, observant, and increasingly volatile, with a private life that suggests pain beneath the silence. Her shift from withdrawn friend to explosive truth-teller gives the character a strong internal arc and a lot of tension.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role actors like because it starts contained and then opens into something more dangerous. Lucy has the stillness, resentment, and eventual eruption that can make a supporting lead memorable in a horror ensemble, especially for an actor who wants to play subtext and then detonate it. The part has the quiet intensity of a character who can steal scenes by withholding.

lead_characters.name: Daniel Stokes-Simpson
lead_characters.hook: Daniel is the easygoing, athletic boyfriend who knows how to calm a room and keep the social machine moving. He’s funny, affectionate, and socially central, but he also serves as the emotional ballast for Faye and the broader group. He’s written as the kind of guy everyone trusts until the horror world starts taking people away.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a strong supporting role for a young actor who can play charm, warmth, and sudden fear in a genre setting. Daniel gets romance, banter, and a meaningful death scene, which gives the part real impact even without being the lead. It’s the kind of role that can make an actor memorable in a crowded ensemble.

lead_characters.name: Ryan
lead_characters.hook: Ryan enters as a quiet outsider with a history of surviving the grandmother’s violence, which gives him instant mystery and credibility. He’s awkward, a little guarded, and unexpectedly flirtatious with Sammy, making him both a witness and a possible emotional complication. He feels like a survivor character with enough edge to matter in the endgame.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a useful role for an actor who can play wounded, suspicious, and unexpectedly charming in the same frame. Ryan has a built-in backstory, a direct connection to the central threat, and a late-story chemistry lane with Sammy that gives the part more than just exposition value. It’s a compact but memorable genre-supporting role.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to stage teen chaos with real bite and no polish.
director_appeal.detail: This material rewards someone who can keep a large ensemble moving while making every confrontation feel personal and dangerous. The movie wants a director who enjoys tonal excess, sharp social behavior, and practical horror set pieces that play hard without needing a giant canvas.

buyer_appeal.detail: This fits a contained, cast-driven horror slot with strong trailer moments, modest locations, and a clear youth audience. It’s the kind of project that can be packaged around a young ensemble rather than star dependency, which makes it attractive for a lower-budget genre buyer.

considerations.area: The feature plays as a high-intensity ensemble slasher.
considerations.detail: The current shape is best positioned as a contained genre feature with a youth-skewing audience and a modest production footprint. The social dynamics are the selling point, so packaging should foreground the ensemble chemistry and the killer mystery rather than a single-star dependency.

considerations.area: The dialogue runs at full volume.
considerations.detail: The script’s voice is one of its defining assets, and a future pass could sharpen the rhythm by protecting the most distinctive lines and trimming repeated beats so the big moments land even harder. The goal would be to keep the same feral energy while making the escalation feel even cleaner.

There are several moving pieces — Katie, Sammy’s grandmother, Lucy’s isolation, the police interrogations, and the friend-group betrayals — and the feature would benefit from keeping the central throughline especially crisp as the body count rises. One direction would be to foreground the killer’s emotional logic a little earlier so the reveal lands with maximum inevitability.

considerations.area: The ensemble is strongest when pairings drive scenes.
considerations.detail: The Austin/Lauren, Sammy/Lucy, and Faye/Daniel dynamics are the most playable engines on the page, and the script should continue to protect those pairings as the story escalates. Leaning into those relationships will keep the horror from feeling purely procedural and will deepen the audience attachment to the victims.

considerations.area: The violence is built for a mature lane.
considerations.detail: The script is firmly in explicit horror territory, with graphic stabbings, throat slits, and repeated chase violence. That makes the project a natural fit for a genre buyer comfortable with harder content and a narrower but very clear audience promise.

considerations.area: The brand references are light but present.
considerations.detail: Named references like McDonald’s, DoorDash, and Get Out are manageable, but they should be kept intentional so they don’t distract from the original voice of the piece. The movie’s identity is strongest when it feels fully owned by its characters and world.
